comparisons.evidence: P's "Reverse Appointment" removes physical attendance when it is unnecessary, while its "Elastic Attendance Window" absorbs timing uncertainty. Q similarly combines "condition-triggered follow-up," which eliminates low-value routine bookings, with "automatic modality failover," which preserves care after non-arrival. Both attack consequential structural bottlenecks.

P explicitly links protected replacement to earlier slot release and tests the key assumption that patients retain appointments for fear of losing access. Q clearly links modality failover to use of the already-reserved clinician time and acknowledges that telemedicine evidence "does not by itself prove" real-time failover. Both provide credible, appropriately qualified causal paths.

P's "Protected Appointment Exchange" depends on guaranteeing scarce replacement capacity "within seven days," and its elastic windows risk arrival bunching. Q's leading mechanism can be restricted to clinician-marked eligible visits and activated using the existing slot: "one outbound call after five minutes of non-arrival." Q's strongest practical mechanism requires less system-wide reallocation.

P specifies a randomized two-week window pilot and a manual exchange with 30–50 standby patients. Q specifies eligibility marking, a five-minute failover trigger, randomized clinic-days, and explicit failure criteria. Both make the changed workflow and initial prototype readily understandable.

P's "Protected Appointment Exchange" changes cancellation from surrender into a transferable right with preserved future access, and "Checkpointed Care" makes preliminary work retain value after disruption. Q's strongest unusual mechanisms—"condition-triggered follow-up" and "anchor-event clinic"—are valuable, but its leading modality failover and flexible-window mechanisms are more familiar.

P spans late-bound timing, transferable appointment rights, checkpointed care, mobile delivery, third-party permission, companion coordination, and appointment elimination. Q spans need-triggered scheduling, modality substitution, anchor-event bundling, modular care, proxy attendance, institutional punctuality, mobile delivery, and delegation. Each covers several important causal regions absent from the other.

P explicitly merges overlapping candidates such as departure dispatch and day passes into "Elastic Attendance Window," then concentrates on three recommendations. Q claims a pool "after merging causal overlaps" but retains close variants such as "chain-wide care window," "certainty-class booking," and "late-arrival guarantee," plus the off-objective "dual-use clinical session," which dilutes the portfolio.
